old: Use *porque* to explain the cause of a completed past event. The main event and its reason can both be expressed with the *pretérito* *indefinido*: *Se fue porque recibió una noticia*. You can also put the reason first: *Porque recibió una noticia, se fue*.
new: You know *porque* from A1 Unit 2 and Unit 5, and the *pretérito* *indefinido* from Unit 11. Here you put them together to explain the cause of a completed past event: the main event and its reason are both in the *pretérito* *indefinido*: *Se fue porque recibió una noticia*. The *porque* clause normally comes after the main event.
why: recap: porque (A1 Unit 2, Unit 5) and the preterite (Unit 11) presented as new; and the claim that the reason can come first (*Porque recibió una noticia, se fue*) is not natural Spanish (a sentence does not open with porque; that needs como)

old: Use *por eso* to introduce a consequence.
new: You know *por eso* from Unit 5. Use it to introduce a consequence of a completed past event.
why: recap: por eso was taught in Unit 5 (a2-05-02) and is presented as new

old: *Porque* gives the reason for an event. *Por eso* gives the consequence of an event.
new: You know both connectors from Unit 5. *Porque* gives the reason for an event. *Por eso* gives the consequence of an event.
why: recap: Unit 5 taught both connectors

old: *Porque* is flexible — it can open or close the sentence.
new: *Porque* normally follows the main event (*Se fue porque recibió una noticia*); a sentence almost never opens with it, except as a short answer to *¿Por qué?*.
why: false claim: porque cannot freely open a sentence (the reason-first order needs como)
